title: Teach the idea before its name
statement: When a later lesson owns a concept's technical name, teach the idea first in plain words and hold the term back, so the name attaches to an idea already held.
detail: Lesson research for a unit's second lesson ruled against giving learners a technical term that the course plan reserves for a later lesson, because the course's knowledge rules want prior knowledge reused rather than re-taught, which works better if the later lesson attaches a new name to a concept already held. The unit's opening film followed the same line: two beats show the idea, how a stranger who knocks is treated, without using the term, and the course plan notes say the film does not have to use the word.
against: Two rules point the other way. The same engine names procedures from the first demonstration, since "a child who has watched FIND four times without once hearing it called FIND has been given four demonstrations and no tool." (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/rules/pedagogy-and-lesson-structure.md`, lines 343-345), and the intro-video rule recorded in name-the-term-and-show-the-instance says to name a term together with its instance, never the instance alone. The sources give no measure of which order teaches better.

evidence.quote: One decision this raises: do not give the child the Greek word xenia at L2. The graph reserves the naming for L6, and R-KC-5 wants prior knowledge reused rather than re-taught, which works better if L6 gets to attach a new name to a concept the child already holds.
